title: How Does a Volcano Erupt?
paragraphs: Imagine standing on a mountainside as the ground beneath your feet begins to rumble. Suddenly, a column of ash and gas shoots high into the sky, and glowing rivers of molten rock pour down the slopes. This is a volcanic eruption, one of the most powerful events in nature. But what makes a volcano erupt? To find the answer, we need to journey deep inside our planet.

The Earth is made up of layers, a little like a peach. On the outside is the crust, a thin skin of solid rock that is thinnest beneath the oceans. Under the crust lies the mantle, a thick layer of extremely hot rock. Although most of the mantle is solid, it is so hot that, over millions of years, it can slowly creep and flow. At the very centre lies the core, made mostly of iron, where temperatures reach thousands of degrees Celsius.

The crust is not one unbroken shell. Instead, it is cracked into enormous pieces called tectonic plates, which fit together like the pieces of a jigsaw. The plates rest on the mantle and move very slowly – only a few centimetres each year, which is about as fast as your fingernails grow. Most volcanoes are found near the edges of plates, where two plates are pulling apart or where one plate is being forced beneath another.

In these places, some of the rock deep underground melts to form magma: hot, liquid rock that contains gases such as water vapour. Because magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, it slowly rises, squeezing through cracks. Often, it collects in a huge underground pool called a magma chamber, which may lie a few kilometres beneath the surface.

As more magma pushes into the chamber, the pressure inside it grows. Eventually, the pressure becomes so great that the magma forces its way up through cracks in the crust. As it rises, there is less rock pressing down on it, so the gases in the magma begin to form bubbles, just as bubbles appear when you open a bottle of fizzy drink. The bubbles push the magma upwards even faster, until it bursts out at the surface through an opening called a vent. Once magma reaches the surface, it is called lava. Lava can be hotter than 1,000 degrees Celsius.

Not all eruptions are alike. When magma is runny, gas escapes from it easily, and lava pours gently out of the volcano like a glowing river. When magma is thick and sticky, however, the gas becomes trapped. The pressure builds and builds until the volcano explodes violently, blasting clouds of ash high into the air. Volcanic ash is nothing like the soft, powdery ash left by a bonfire: it is made of tiny, sharp pieces of rock and glass. In 2010, ash from an eruption in Iceland drifted across Europe, and tens of thousands of flights were cancelled because the ash could damage aircraft engines.

Each time a volcano erupts, its lava and ash cool and harden into new rock. Eruption after eruption, layer upon layer builds up, forming the cone shape that many volcanoes have. Scientists describe volcanoes as active, dormant or extinct. An active volcano has erupted recently or may erupt soon. A dormant volcano has been quiet for a long time but could erupt again, while an extinct volcano is not expected ever to erupt again. Edinburgh Castle, in Scotland, stands on the remains of a volcano that has been extinct for millions of years.

Despite the dangers, millions of people around the world live close to volcanoes. The soil on their slopes is often extremely rich, because volcanic ash and rock break down into minerals that help plants to grow, so farmers can harvest plentiful crops. In Iceland, heat from deep underground warms most people’s homes. To keep people safe, scientists called volcanologists watch active volcanoes closely. They measure tiny earthquakes, check whether the ground is swelling as magma pushes up beneath it and test the gases escaping from the vent. These clues can give people time to leave their homes before an eruption begins.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 1.
Find and copy **one** word that means melted.

Look at paragraphs 2 and 3.
Using information from these paragraphs, decide whether each statement is true or false.
statements: The crust is thinnest beneath the oceans.
Most of the mantle is liquid.
The Earth’s core is made mostly of iron.
Tectonic plates move a few metres each year.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 3.
Find and copy one word that means extremely large.

Look at paragraph 3.
Using the information in this paragraph, where would you be least likely to find a volcano? Tick one.
options: where two plates are pulling apart
where one plate is being forced beneath another
in the middle of a plate, far from its edges
near the edge of a plate

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 5.
Why does the writer compare the gas bubbles in magma to the bubbles in a bottle of fizzy drink? Tick one.
options: to help the reader picture something they cannot see by comparing it with something familiar
to suggest that volcanoes are harmless
to show that magma is cold
to explain why magma can be thick and sticky

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 5.
What is the opening that magma bursts out through called?

Look at paragraph 6.
What does the eruption in Iceland in 2010 show about volcanoes? Tick one.
options: Volcanoes only affect the country they are in.
Volcanic ash is soft and harmless.
Aircraft can fly safely through volcanic ash.
An eruption can affect people who live far away from the volcano.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 6.
Explain how an eruption of runny magma is different from an eruption of thick, sticky magma.
questions.model: When magma is runny, the gas escapes from it easily, so the lava pours gently out of the volcano like a glowing river. When magma is thick and sticky, the gas becomes trapped, so the pressure builds up until the volcano explodes violently and blasts clouds of ash high into the air.
points: what happens with runny magma (1 mark), e.g. the gas escapes easily; the lava pours gently out “like a glowing river”.
what happens with thick, sticky magma (1 mark), e.g. the gas is trapped and the pressure builds up; the volcano “explodes violently”, blasting clouds of ash high into the air.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 7.
Which building in Scotland stands on the remains of an extinct volcano?

Look at paragraph 8.
…check whether the ground is **swelling** as magma pushes up beneath it…
Which word is closest in meaning to **swelling**? Tick one.
options: shaking
sinking
bulging
cooling

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 8.
Why do you think so many people live close to volcanoes, even though volcanoes can be dangerous? Explain, using evidence from the text.
questions.model: I think people live near volcanoes because the land is useful to them. The text says that “the soil on their slopes is often extremely rich”, so “farmers can harvest plentiful crops”. In Iceland, “heat from deep underground warms most people’s homes”. People may also feel safer because volcanologists “watch active volcanoes closely”, and “these clues can give people time to leave their homes before an eruption begins”.
points: A reason about farming, e.g. the rich soil helps farmers grow plentiful crops
A reason about heat, e.g. in Iceland, heat from underground warms people’s homes
A reason about safety, e.g. volcanologists watch volcanoes and can warn people in time to leave

questions.prompt: Number these stages from 1 to 5 to show the order in which they happen.
items: Magma bursts out at the surface.
Rock deep underground melts to form magma.
Lava and ash cool and harden into new rock.
Magma collects in a magma chamber.
Pressure builds up and gas bubbles form.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer explain what the inside of the Earth is like (paragraphs 2 and 3) before describing how a volcano erupts? Tick one.
options: because the layers of the Earth are more exciting than eruptions
because the text tells the story of the writer’s visit to a volcano
because volcanoes only form in the Earth’s core
because readers need to know what is inside the Earth to understand where magma comes from

questions.prompt: Which of these is the best summary of the whole text? Tick one.
options: Volcanoes are only found in Iceland and Scotland, where they erupt every year.
Volcanoes erupt when magma from deep underground rises and bursts out under pressure; eruptions can be dangerous, but scientists watch volcanoes closely.
Most of the Earth is made of liquid rock, which is why volcanoes erupt.
Volcanoes erupt because the Earth’s core breaks through the crust.
